frontHtml: Why does X-linked agammaglobulinemia present after about 6 months of age?
backHtml: Transplacental maternal IgG (half-life about 3–4 weeks) protects until it wanes; the infant cannot make his own.

frontHtml: At which developmental stage are B cells arrested in BTK deficiency?
backHtml: Pro-B/pre-B stage in the marrow; pre-B receptor signalling fails, so circulating CD19+ cells are below about 2%.

frontHtml: Which viral infection is characteristic of X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and why?
backHtml: Chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis (and vaccine polio); enterovirus clearance depends on neutralizing antibody.

frontHtml: In CVID, are B cells usually present, and what fails?
backHtml: Usually present; terminal differentiation into plasma cells fails, with reduced class-switched memory B cells.

frontHtml: Name four noninfectious complications of CVID.
backHtml: Autoimmune cytopenias (ITP, AIHA), granulomatous disease/GLILD, enteropathy, lymphoma and gastric cancer.

frontHtml: What compensates mucosally in selective IgA deficiency?
backHtml: Secretory IgM, which carries a J chain and is transported by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor.

frontHtml: How does AID-deficient hyper-IgM differ from CD40L deficiency?
backHtml: AID: autosomal recessive, giant germinal centres, no opportunistic infections. CD40L: X-linked, no germinal centres, Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium.

frontHtml: Why do conjugate vaccines work in specific antibody deficiency?
backHtml: The protein carrier recruits T-cell help, converting a T-independent polysaccharide response into a T-dependent one.

frontHtml: Which cytokine receptors share the common γ chain?
backHtml: Six cytokine receptors use it: those for IL-2, -4, -7, -9, -15 and -21 (gene IL2RG, X-linked).

frontHtml: Lineage phenotype of IL2RG or JAK3 SCID?
backHtml: T−B+NK− (IL-7 loss removes T cells; IL-15 loss removes NK cells).

frontHtml: Lineage phenotype of RAG1/2 or Artemis SCID?
backHtml: T−B−NK+, because V(D)J recombination is needed only by T and B cells.

frontHtml: Which metabolite kills lymphocytes in ADA deficiency?
backHtml: dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase.

frontHtml: Features of Omenn syndrome?
backHtml: Leaky (hypomorphic RAG) SCID: erythroderma, alopecia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, eosinophilia, high IgE, absent B cells, oligoclonal T cells.

frontHtml: What do TRECs measure on the newborn screen?
backHtml: Recent thymic output: excised DNA circles from TCR rearrangement that do not replicate.

frontHtml: Which lymph node zone is depleted in T-cell aplasia?
backHtml: The paracortex.

frontHtml: What does WAS protein do?
backHtml: Links receptor signalling to actin polymerisation (Arp2/3) in hematopoietic cells.

frontHtml: Immunoglobulin pattern in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
backHtml: Low IgM, high IgA and IgE, often normal IgG; poor polysaccharide responses.

frontHtml: Which serum marker is raised in ataxia-telangiectasia?
backHtml: α-Fetoprotein.

frontHtml: What is the function of ATM?
backHtml: Sensing DNA double-strand breaks and activating checkpoints and repair; loss causes radiosensitivity.

frontHtml: Serum IFN-γ in complete IFN-γ receptor deficiency versus IL-12Rβ1 deficiency?
backHtml: High in receptor deficiency (unused ligand); low in IL-12Rβ1 deficiency.

frontHtml: Most frequent genetic cause of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis?
backHtml: STAT1 gain-of-function mutations.

frontHtml: Why do patients with APECED get candidiasis?
backHtml: Neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-17 and IL-22.

frontHtml: Which T-cell subset fails in STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome?
backHtml: Th17 cells (IL-6 and IL-23 signalling require STAT3).

frontHtml: Distinguishing features of DOCK8 deficiency?
backHtml: Autosomal recessive hyper-IgE with severe cutaneous viral infections (HSV, HPV, molluscum), food allergy and early malignancy.

frontHtml: Why does early classical complement deficiency cause lupus?
backHtml: Apoptotic cells and immune complexes are not cleared, so nuclear antigens persist and drive autoimmunity.

frontHtml: Rank C1q, C4 and C2 deficiency by lupus risk.
backHtml: C1q highest, then C4, then C2.

frontHtml: CH50 normal, AH50 low: which components?
backHtml: Factor B, factor D or properdin.

frontHtml: CH50 and AH50 both low: which components?
backHtml: C3 or C5–C9, or C3 consumption from factor H or I loss.

frontHtml: Inheritance and presentation of properdin deficiency?
backHtml: X-linked; fulminant meningococcal disease in boys.

frontHtml: Which factor H defect causes atypical HUS?
backHtml: Variants impairing factor H binding to host-cell surfaces (C-terminal domains), so C3b is not regulated on endothelium.

frontHtml: C1-INH protein and function in HAE types I and II?
backHtml: Type I: low protein, low function. Type II: normal or high protein, low function. C4 low in both.

frontHtml: Which complement test separates acquired from hereditary C1-INH deficiency?
backHtml: C1q: low in acquired, normal in hereditary.

frontHtml: Mechanism of eculizumab and its main infectious risk?
backHtml: Binds C5 and prevents cleavage (no C5a or MAC); meningococcal disease.

frontHtml: Most frequent and most severe genetic form of CGD?
backHtml: X-linked CYBB (gp91phox).

frontHtml: Five classic CGD pathogens?
backHtml: S. aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus.

frontHtml: Which skin finding is seen in carriers of X-linked CGD?
backHtml: Photosensitive discoid-lupus-like lesions (also aphthous ulcers).

frontHtml: Protein and step lost in LAD-1?
backHtml: CD18 (β2 integrin); firm adhesion to ICAM-1 and transmigration.

frontHtml: Defect and blood-group finding in LAD-2?
backHtml: GDP-fucose transporter (SLC35C1): absent sialyl Lewis X and Bombay (hh) phenotype.

frontHtml: Gene and smear finding in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?
backHtml: LYST; giant granules in neutrophils and other cells.

frontHtml: Which infection occurs in symptomatic MPO deficiency?
backHtml: Invasive Candida, mainly in patients with diabetes.

frontHtml: Marrow finding and gene in severe congenital neutropenia?
backHtml: Maturation arrest at the promyelocyte–myelocyte stage; ELANE most frequent.

frontHtml: Cycle length in cyclic neutropenia?
backHtml: About 21 days.

frontHtml: Why does perforin deficiency cause hyperinflammation?
backHtml: Cytotoxic cells cannot kill targets, so stimulation and IFN-γ release continue unchecked (familial HLH).

frontHtml: First immunologic test for recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infection?
backHtml: Quantitative IgG, IgA and IgM against age-specific ranges (with CBC and HIV test).

frontHtml: When must vaccine titers be measured relative to IgG replacement?
backHtml: Before starting it; infused IgG contains donor antibodies and masks the result.

frontHtml: Usual starting dose of IgG replacement in primary antibody deficiency?
backHtml: About 400–600 mg/kg every 4 weeks (IV), or the equivalent weekly SCIG, adjusted to clinical response.

frontHtml: Name three systemic adverse effects of IVIG.
backHtml: Aseptic meningitis, thrombosis, acute kidney injury (sucrose products), hemolysis, headache.

frontHtml: Celiac serology in IgA deficiency?
backHtml: IgG-based: tissue transglutaminase IgG or deamidated gliadin peptide IgG.

frontHtml: Blood products for an IgA-deficient patient with prior anti-IgA anaphylaxis?
backHtml: Washed cellular products, or products from IgA-deficient donors (plasma must come from IgA-deficient donors).

frontHtml: Is IVIG indicated for isolated selective IgA deficiency?
backHtml: No; it cannot replace secretory IgA and may provoke reactions.

frontHtml: Next test after an absent TREC on newborn screening?
backHtml: Lymphocyte subset flow cytometry including naive T cells.

frontHtml: Which routine infant live vaccine is contraindicated in SCID?
backHtml: Rotavirus vaccine (and BCG where given).

frontHtml: Blood products for an infant with suspected T-cell deficiency?
backHtml: Irradiated, leukoreduced, CMV-safe cellular products.

frontHtml: Timing that gives the best HSCT survival in SCID?
backHtml: Within the first 3.5 months and before infection.

frontHtml: Bridge therapy specific to ADA-SCID?
backHtml: PEG-conjugated ADA enzyme replacement (elapegademase); gene therapy is an alternative.

frontHtml: Treatment of complete athymia in 22q11.2 deletion?
backHtml: Cultured thymus tissue implantation.

frontHtml: Why is splenectomy avoided in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
backHtml: It greatly increases overwhelming sepsis; HSCT is preferred.

frontHtml: Which endocrine test is essential in APECED follow-up?
backHtml: Morning cortisol and ACTH (adrenal insufficiency), plus calcium and PTH.

frontHtml: Best initial test for angioedema without urticaria?
backHtml: Serum C4.

frontHtml: On-demand HAE therapies?
backHtml: IV C1-INH (plasma-derived or recombinant), subcutaneous icatibant, ecallantide.

frontHtml: Preprocedural HAE prophylaxis?
backHtml: Plasma-derived C1-INH concentrate 1–6 hours before the procedure.

frontHtml: Long-term HAE prophylaxis options?
backHtml: Subcutaneous C1-INH, lanadelumab, oral berotralstat; androgens second-line (not in children or pregnancy).

frontHtml: Drugs to avoid in HAE?
backHtml: Estrogen-containing contraceptives and hormone therapy, and ACE inhibitors.

frontHtml: Which antihypertensives are contraindicated after ACE-inhibitor angioedema?
backHtml: All ACE inhibitors and sacubitril-valsartan; ARBs only with caution.

frontHtml: Vaccines before starting a C5 inhibitor?
backHtml: Meningococcal vaccines (both ACWY and serogroup B) given 2 or more weeks ahead; if the drug cannot wait, cover with antibiotics until 2 weeks after vaccination.

frontHtml: Why repeat a low CH50 before further testing?
backHtml: Complement is heat-labile; delayed or warm handling gives falsely low values.

frontHtml: Standard prophylaxis in CGD?
backHtml: Daily TMP-SMX and itraconazole, with optional interferon-γ three times weekly.

frontHtml: Which vaccines are contraindicated in CGD?
backHtml: Live bacterial vaccines (BCG, oral typhoid); live viral vaccines are safe.

frontHtml: How can MPO deficiency mimic CGD on testing?
backHtml: It can reduce the DHR signal; a normal NBT or oxidase assay and absent peroxidase staining identify MPO deficiency.

frontHtml: Confirmatory test for LAD-1?
backHtml: Flow cytometry for CD18 (and CD11) on leukocytes.

frontHtml: How is cyclic neutropenia documented?
backHtml: Serial CBCs two or three times weekly for about 6 weeks.

frontHtml: Treatment and surveillance in severe congenital neutropenia?
backHtml: Daily G-CSF; yearly marrow with cytogenetics for MDS/AML; HSCT for nonresponders or transformation.

frontHtml: Induction therapy for familial HLH?
backHtml: Dexamethasone and etoposide (HLH-94 based), intrathecal therapy for CNS disease, then HSCT.

frontHtml: Malignancy risk in GATA2 deficiency?
backHtml: Myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia.

frontHtml: Which HIV protein binds CD4, and which mediates membrane fusion?
backHtml: gp120 binds CD4 (then a CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptor); gp41 drives fusion.

frontHtml: What does homozygous CCR5-Δ32 do to HIV susceptibility?
backHtml: No surface CCR5, so R5 (the usually transmitted) virus cannot enter: strong protection.

frontHtml: Which HIV antigen is detected by 4th-generation screening assays?
backHtml: p24 capsid antigen (plus anti-HIV-1/2 antibodies).

frontHtml: What host restriction factor does HIV Vif target?
backHtml: APOBEC3G, which would otherwise hypermutate viral DNA.

frontHtml: Why does HIV-2 respond poorly to efavirenz?
backHtml: HIV-2 reverse transcriptase has a different NNRTI-binding pocket; NNRTIs (and enfuvirtide) have little activity.

frontHtml: Which HIV enzyme do integrase strand-transfer inhibitors block, and at what step?
backHtml: Integrase; they stop insertion of viral DNA into the host genome.

frontHtml: Which HLA allele must be excluded before starting abacavir?
backHtml: HLA-B*57:01 (risk of a hypersensitivity reaction).

frontHtml: Kaposi sarcoma is driven by which virus?
backHtml: HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus).

frontHtml: Classic biopsy pattern of HIV-associated nephropathy?
backHtml: Collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with tubular microcysts.

frontHtml: Name the renal and bone toxicities more typical of tenofovir disoproxil than tenofovir alafenamide.
backHtml: Proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi-like) and loss of bone mineral density.

frontHtml: Why is maraviroc used only after a tropism assay?
backHtml: It blocks CCR5 only, so it works only against R5-tropic virus.

frontHtml: What CD4 count pattern characterizes untreated HIV over years?
backHtml: Steady decline after acute infection; AIDS-defining infections mostly below 200/mm³.

frontHtml: Type I hypersensitivity: trigger for mast cell degranulation?
backHtml: Cross-linking of allergen-specific IgE bound to FcεRI.

frontHtml: Type II hypersensitivity: what is the antibody target?
backHtml: A fixed antigen on a cell surface or matrix (e.g. desmoglein in pemphigus vulgaris).

frontHtml: Arthus reaction: type and timing?
backHtml: Local type III (immune-complex) vasculitis, peaking about 4–12 hours after antigen.

frontHtml: Allergic contact dermatitis: type, timing and effector?
backHtml: Type IV; 24–72 hours; hapten-sensitized T cells.

frontHtml: Which cytokine drives eosinophils in the late-phase allergic response?
backHtml: IL-5 (from Th2 cells and ILC2s).

frontHtml: Delayed anaphylaxis 3–6 hours after red meat after tick bites: what is the allergen?
backHtml: Galactose-α-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal), a mammalian carbohydrate.

frontHtml: Probability that a full sibling is HLA-identical?
backHtml: 25% (50% haploidentical, 25% no shared haplotype).

frontHtml: Hyperacute rejection: mechanism and timing?
backHtml: Preformed antibodies (ABO, anti-HLA) with complement and thrombosis, within minutes to hours.

frontHtml: Biopsy marker of antibody-mediated rejection?
backHtml: C4d along peritubular capillaries, with capillaritis and donor-specific antibodies.

frontHtml: Lung transplant chronic rejection appears as what?
backHtml: Bronchiolitis obliterans: progressive obstruction with fibrous obliteration of bronchioles.

frontHtml: Acute GVHD target organs after stem cell transplant?
backHtml: Skin (palms, soles, ears first), gut (diarrhea) and liver (cholestasis).

frontHtml: Which donor/recipient CMV pairing has the highest risk?
backHtml: Donor seropositive, recipient seronegative (D+/R−).

frontHtml: Tacrolimus: binding protein and enzyme inhibited?
backHtml: Binds FKBP12; inhibits calcineurin, so NFAT cannot drive IL-2 transcription.

frontHtml: Sirolimus: target and signature adverse effects?
backHtml: mTORC1; hyperlipidemia, poor wound healing, mouth ulcers, cytopenias, pneumonitis; not nephrotoxic.

frontHtml: Why is mycophenolate relatively lymphocyte-selective?
backHtml: It inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, and lymphocytes rely on de novo guanine synthesis.

frontHtml: Azathioprine + allopurinol: what happens and why?
backHtml: Xanthine oxidase inhibition raises 6-mercaptopurine levels, causing myelosuppression.

frontHtml: Which genes are checked before thiopurines?
backHtml: TPMT (and NUDT15); low activity causes severe myelosuppression.

frontHtml: Which antibiotic class raises tacrolimus levels through CYP3A4 inhibition?
backHtml: Macrolides such as clarithromycin and erythromycin (azithromycin much less).

frontHtml: Why do TNF inhibitors reactivate tuberculosis?
backHtml: TNF is needed to form and maintain granulomas.

frontHtml: Rituximab and new non-enhancing white-matter lesions with focal deficits: diagnosis?
backHtml: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus).

frontHtml: Fever and rigors hours after the first penicillin dose for syphilis?
backHtml: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (cytokines from dying spirochetes); not an allergy.

frontHtml: Which checkpoint target is most associated with hypophysitis?
backHtml: CTLA-4 (ipilimumab), especially in combination therapy.

frontHtml: Omalizumab binds what?
backHtml: Free IgE (Fc region), preventing binding to FcεRI.

frontHtml: Which hepatitis B marker predicts reactivation risk with rituximab even when HBsAg is negative?
backHtml: Positive hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc).

frontHtml: Reactive Ag/Ab screen, negative differentiation assay: next test?
backHtml: HIV-1 RNA; positive means acute HIV-1 infection.

frontHtml: Is the Western blot part of the current HIV testing algorithm?
backHtml: No; the differentiation immunoassay replaced it.

frontHtml: When should ART start after HIV diagnosis?
backHtml: As soon as possible, ideally within days, whatever the CD4 count.

frontHtml: Baseline tests at HIV diagnosis besides CD4 and viral load?
backHtml: Resistance genotype, HLA-B*57:01 if abacavir is considered, hepatitis B and C, kidney and liver function, STI screening.

frontHtml: Should ART wait for resistance results?
backHtml: No; start a high-barrier regimen and adjust if needed.

frontHtml: Why test for hepatitis B before choosing ART?
backHtml: Regimens for coinfection must include drugs active against HBV (e.g. tenofovir); stopping them can cause a flare.

frontHtml: What must be done before starting HIV PrEP?
backHtml: Confirm HIV-negative status (Ag/Ab test, plus RNA after recent exposure).

frontHtml: PEP: how soon and for how long?
backHtml: As soon as possible (within 72 hours), three drugs for 28 days.

frontHtml: CD4 below 200/mm³: which prophylaxis?
backHtml: Pneumocystis prophylaxis, usually trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

frontHtml: CD4 below 100/mm³ with positive Toxoplasma IgG: prophylaxis?
backHtml: TMP-SMX daily (covers Toxoplasma and Pneumocystis).

frontHtml: Paradoxical IRIS after ART: continue or stop ART?
backHtml: Continue ART and pathogen therapy; treat inflammation (NSAIDs, prednisone if moderate–severe).

frontHtml: HIV diagnosed in pregnancy: when to start ART?
backHtml: Immediately, whatever the CD4 count or trimester.

frontHtml: First drug for anaphylaxis, route and site?
backHtml: Epinephrine intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes as needed.

frontHtml: Do antihistamines or glucocorticoids treat anaphylactic shock?
backHtml: No; they are adjuncts and do not replace epinephrine.

frontHtml: Discharge essentials after anaphylaxis?
backHtml: Two epinephrine autoinjectors with training, an action plan, allergen avoidance and allergist follow-up.

frontHtml: Which lab test supports mast cell activation after a suspected anaphylactic episode?
backHtml: Serum tryptase, drawn within a few hours, compared with a baseline level.

frontHtml: Infant with mild eczema: when to introduce peanut?
backHtml: Around 4–6 months, at home, in an age-appropriate form.

frontHtml: Biphasic anaphylaxis means what?
backHtml: Symptoms return hours later without re-exposure; observe and give autoinjectors.

frontHtml: Low-risk penicillin allergy history: evaluation?
backHtml: Direct oral amoxicillin challenge with observation, then remove the label.

frontHtml: Syphilis in pregnancy with true penicillin allergy?
backHtml: Desensitize, then treat with penicillin.

frontHtml: SJS versus TEN by body surface area detached?
backHtml: SJS below 10%; overlap 10–30%; TEN above 30%.

frontHtml: Most important first step in SJS/TEN?
backHtml: Stop the culprit drug; supportive care in a burn or intensive care unit.

frontHtml: DRESS: timing and key features?
backHtml: 2–8 weeks after a drug; fever, rash, facial edema, eosinophilia, organ involvement.

frontHtml: Which HLA allele raises severe reaction risk with allopurinol?
Rising creatinine after kidney transplant with normal Doppler, drug levels and BK PCR: next step?
backHtml: Allograft biopsy.

frontHtml: Most common cancer after solid-organ transplant?
backHtml: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Tissue-invasive CMV after transplant: treatment?
backHtml: Intravenous ganciclovir (valganciclovir for milder disease); foscarnet for resistance.

frontHtml: When are live vaccines given to transplant candidates?
backHtml: At least 4 weeks before transplant; contraindicated afterward.

frontHtml: Tremor, hyperkalemia and rising creatinine after clarithromycin in a tacrolimus user?
backHtml: CYP3A4 inhibition raised tacrolimus levels; stop the macrolide and hold or reduce tacrolimus.

frontHtml: First step in EBV-positive PTLD management?
backHtml: Reduce immunosuppression; add rituximab for CD20+ disease.

frontHtml: Screening before a TNF inhibitor?
backHtml: Latent TB (IGRA) and hepatitis B serologies; update vaccines first.

frontHtml: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, starting rituximab?
backHtml: Antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir or tenofovir) before and for at least 12 months after.

frontHtml: Severe checkpoint-inhibitor colitis: management?
backHtml: Hold the drug, systemic glucocorticoids; infliximab or vedolizumab if refractory.

frontHtml: Hypophysitis from a checkpoint inhibitor: hormone order?
backHtml: Glucocorticoid first, then thyroid hormone.

frontHtml: Mouth ulcers and mild ALT rise on weekly methotrexate?
backHtml: Add folic acid and continue with monitoring.

frontHtml: Shingles vaccine for an adult on infliximab?
backHtml: Recombinant adjuvanted zoster vaccine (non-live); live vaccines are contraindicated.

frontHtml: Which Plasmodium species form liver hypnozoites, and what do they cause?
backHtml: P. vivax and P. ovale; dormant hypnozoites cause relapse weeks to months later, so radical cure needs primaquine or tafenoquine after G6PD testing.

frontHtml: Which erythrocyte receptor does P. vivax use to invade, and which cells does it prefer?
backHtml: The Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines; it prefers reticulocytes, so parasitemia stays low.

frontHtml: What parasite protein mediates P. falciparum cytoadherence, and what are its endothelial ligands?
backHtml: PfEMP1 on red cell surface knobs, binding ICAM-1, EPCR and CD36 in post-capillary venules.

frontHtml: How does chloroquine kill blood-stage parasites?
backHtml: Concentrated as a weak base in the acidic food vacuole, it prevents polymerization of free heme into hemozoin, so toxic heme accumulates.

frontHtml: Name two smear features that separate Babesia from Plasmodium.
backHtml: Babesia forms cross-shaped tetrads and produces no pigment and no gametocytes.

frontHtml: Which cell does parvovirus B19 infect, through which receptor, and with what haematologic result?
backHtml: Erythroid progenitors via the P antigen (globoside); erythropoiesis pauses for 1-2 weeks, causing aplastic crisis with reticulocytopenia in chronic hemolysis.

frontHtml: Morulae in neutrophils versus morulae in monocytes: which organism and which tick?
backHtml: Neutrophils: Anaplasma phagocytophilum (Ixodes). Monocytes: Ehrlichia chaffeensis (Amblyomma americanum).

frontHtml: What initiates disseminated intravascular coagulation in Gram-negative sepsis?
backHtml: Endotoxin and cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha) induce tissue factor on monocytes and endothelium, triggering widespread thrombin generation.

frontHtml: What is the best initial test for fever in a traveller returning from an endemic area?
backHtml: Thick and thin blood smears with a rapid antigen test, repeated every 12-24 hours for three sets if negative.

frontHtml: Name four criteria that define severe falciparum malaria.
backHtml: Impaired consciousness or seizures, acidosis or respiratory distress, acute kidney injury or hypoglycemia, and parasitemia above about 5-10% (also shock, severe anemia, jaundice with organ dysfunction).

frontHtml: Treatment of severe falciparum malaria?
backHtml: Intravenous artesunate at any age and in pregnancy, then a full oral artemisinin-based combination course; monitor for delayed post-artesunate hemolysis.

frontHtml: First-line therapy for mild to moderate babesiosis, and for severe disease?
backHtml: Atovaquone plus azithromycin; severe disease gets intravenous clindamycin plus quinine, with red cell exchange transfusion considered.

frontHtml: Why is doxycycline started before test results in suspected anaplasmosis or ehrlichiosis?
backHtml: Confirmatory PCR and serology take days and delay worsens outcome; fever usually settles within 48 hours of doxycycline.

frontHtml: Management of transient aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19?
backHtml: Simple red cell transfusion for symptomatic anemia with droplet precautions, until reticulocytes recover in 1-2 weeks.

frontHtml: In sepsis-associated DIC, when are blood products given?
backHtml: For bleeding or before procedures, not to normalize numbers; antifibrinolytics are avoided and source control is the priority.

frontHtml: Which nodal compartment expands in viral infection, and with which cells?
backHtml: The paracortex (T zone), with immunoblasts and prominent high endothelial venules.

frontHtml: What are the atypical lymphocytes of infectious mononucleosis?
backHtml: Reactive activated CD8+ cytotoxic T cells responding to EBV-infected B cells, not infected B cells themselves.

frontHtml: What do heterophile antibodies detect, and when is the test unreliable?
backHtml: IgM from polyclonal B-cell activation that agglutinates sheep or horse red cells; it can be negative in the first week and in young children.

frontHtml: Which EBV serologic pattern indicates acute primary infection?
backHtml: IgM against the viral capsid antigen is present, while antibody to the nuclear antigen (EBNA) has not yet appeared.

frontHtml: Where does cytomegalovirus remain latent?
backHtml: In monocytes and CD34+ myeloid progenitors, which is why it is transmitted by cellular blood products and transplanted organs.

frontHtml: Node histology of cat-scratch disease versus acute toxoplasmosis?
backHtml: Cat-scratch: necrotizing granulomas with stellate neutrophilic microabscesses. Toxoplasmosis: follicular hyperplasia, epithelioid histiocyte clusters and monocytoid B cells.

frontHtml: Two patterns of mycobacterial cervical adenitis and their tests?
backHtml: Tuberculous scrofula: matted nodes, caseating granulomas, positive IGRA. Nontuberculous (toddlers): solitary painless node with violaceous skin and negative IGRA.

frontHtml: Why does splenic rupture refer pain to the shoulder tip?
backHtml: Subdiaphragmatic blood irritates diaphragmatic peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), referring pain to the C4 dermatome.

frontHtml: List five red flags in evaluating lymphadenopathy.
backHtml: Size above 2 cm, hard or fixed node, supraclavicular location, age above 40 years, duration beyond 4-6 weeks or B symptoms.

frontHtml: Why is excisional biopsy preferred over fine-needle aspiration when lymphoma is suspected?
backHtml: Classification depends on architecture as well as immunophenotype; aspiration cytology cannot show the growth pattern and a negative result does not exclude lymphoma.

frontHtml: Return-to-play advice after infectious mononucleosis?
backHtml: No contact or collision sports or heavy lifting for at least 3 weeks from symptom onset and while the spleen remains palpable.

frontHtml: Which antibiotics should be avoided in mononucleosis, and why?
backHtml: Amoxicillin and ampicillin, which commonly cause a morbilliform rash.

frontHtml: Treatment of nontuberculous mycobacterial cervical adenitis in a toddler?
backHtml: Complete surgical excision; a macrolide-based regimen if excision risks the facial nerve. Avoid incision and drainage.

frontHtml: When is cat-scratch disease treated with antibiotics?
backHtml: Bulky or uncomfortable adenopathy (azithromycin), immunocompromised patients, and systemic disease such as hepatosplenic abscesses, neuroretinitis or endocarditis.

frontHtml: Does acute toxoplasmic lymphadenitis need treatment?
backHtml: Not in an immunocompetent, non-pregnant adult; pregnancy and immunocompromise do require therapy.

frontHtml: Which gene defects cause familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis?
backHtml: Biallelic defects of the cytotoxic granule pathway: PRF1 (perforin), UNC13D, STX11, STXBP2, and the pigmentary syndromes Chediak-Higashi and Griscelli type 2.

frontHtml: What is the central cytokine of hemophagocytic syndromes, and which cells secrete it?
backHtml: Interferon-gamma, from persistently activated T cells; it drives macrophage hyperactivation with IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha and ferritin release.

frontHtml: Why are triglycerides high and fibrinogen low in HLH?
backHtml: TNF-alpha inhibits lipoprotein lipase, raising triglycerides, while consumptive coagulopathy depletes fibrinogen.

frontHtml: Which laboratory trend betrays macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA?
backHtml: Platelet count, leukocyte count, fibrinogen and ESR fall while ferritin, aminotransferases, triglycerides and D-dimer rise.

frontHtml: Which cytokine and which virus drive multicentric Castleman disease in HIV infection?
backHtml: Interleukin-6 (including a viral IL-6 homolog) produced by HHV-8-infected plasmablasts.

frontHtml: Which cell surface markers and ultrastructural feature identify Langerhans cell histiocytosis?
backHtml: CD1a, langerin (CD207) and S100, with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy; most carry BRAF V600E.

frontHtml: What immunologic defect underlies autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, and what cells accumulate?
backHtml: Impaired FAS-mediated extrinsic apoptosis; alpha-beta double-negative (CD4-CD8-) T cells expand.

frontHtml: Histologic hallmark of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease?
backHtml: Patchy paracortical necrosis with abundant karyorrhectic debris, crescentic histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and no neutrophils.

frontHtml: Which laboratory value should be sent early when hemophagocytic syndrome is suspected?
backHtml: Ferritin; values in the thousands, especially above 10,000 ng/mL, strongly support the diagnosis.

frontHtml: Name four supporting criteria for HLH besides fever and splenomegaly.
backHtml: Bicytopenia or pancytopenia, triglycerides above about 265 mg/dL, fibrinogen below about 150 mg/dL, raised soluble CD25 (also low NK activity and hemophagocytosis).

frontHtml: Backbone of HLH treatment, and what is added for severe or EBV-driven disease?
backHtml: Corticosteroids, with etoposide in severe disease and rituximab added for EBV-driven disease; emapalumab is approved for primary HLH.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of macrophage activation syndrome in rheumatic disease?
backHtml: High-dose corticosteroids with anakinra or cyclosporine; etoposide is reserved for refractory cases.

frontHtml: Treatment of unicentric versus HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease?
backHtml: Unicentric: surgical excision. HHV-8-associated multicentric: rituximab plus antiretroviral therapy. Idiopathic multicentric: siltuximab.

frontHtml: Treatment of multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and of its diabetes insipidus?
backHtml: Systemic chemotherapy, conventionally vinblastine with prednisone; desmopressin for the usually permanent central diabetes insipidus.

frontHtml: Management of asymptomatic stage I sarcoidosis?
backHtml: Observation with monitoring of symptoms, spirometry and diffusing capacity, calcium, creatinine, liver tests, an ECG and ophthalmologic examination.

frontHtml: Why are splenectomy and rituximab avoided where possible in ALPS?
backHtml: Splenectomy risks overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis, and rituximab causes prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia; sirolimus or mycophenolate are preferred for cytopenias.

frontHtml: Which enzyme confirms lymphoblastic lineage, and what does it do?
backHtml: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, which adds untemplated nucleotides at antigen receptor junctions in lymphoid precursors.

frontHtml: Favourable and unfavourable genetics in childhood B-lymphoblastic leukemia?
backHtml: Favourable: hyperdiploidy, ETV6::RUNX1, age 1-9 years. Unfavourable: infancy with KMT2A rearrangement, hypodiploidy, BCR::ABL1.

frontHtml: What are Auer rods made of?
backHtml: Fused primary (azurophilic) granules rich in myeloperoxidase, confirming myeloid lineage.

frontHtml: Which prior chemotherapy causes therapy-related AML with loss of chromosome 5 or 7, and after how long?
backHtml: Alkylating agents, typically 5-7 years later; topoisomerase II inhibitors cause earlier disease with KMT2A rearrangement.

frontHtml: Why are there cytopenias despite a hypercellular marrow in myelodysplastic syndrome?
backHtml: Ineffective hematopoiesis: the clone proliferates but dysplastic progenitors undergo apoptosis before reaching the blood.

frontHtml: Which mutations drive primary myelofibrosis, and who lays down the fibrosis?
backHtml: JAK2 V617F, CALR or MPL; clonal megakaryocytes release TGF-beta and PDGF that stimulate non-neoplastic fibroblasts.

frontHtml: How do you separate the two CD5-positive mature B-cell neoplasms?
backHtml: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is CD23 positive; mantle cell lymphoma is CD23 negative with t(11;14) and cyclin D1.

frontHtml: How does HTLV-1 transform T cells, and what phenotype results?
backHtml: Tax activates NF-kappa B and IL-2/IL-2 receptor transcription; the tumour is clonal CD4+ CD25+ with hypercalcemia and skin involvement.

frontHtml: Which lymphoma arises from chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis, and from Sjogren disease?
backHtml: Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, of stomach and salivary gland respectively.

frontHtml: When is treatment indicated in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
backHtml: Progressive anemia or thrombocytopenia, bulky or symptomatic nodes or spleen, rapid lymphocyte doubling, constitutional symptoms, or steroid-refractory autoimmune cytopenias.

frontHtml: Name three myeloma-defining events besides lytic lesions.
backHtml: Hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency attributable to the clone, anemia (also 60% or more plasma cells, light chain ratio 100 or more, or more than one focal MRI lesion).

frontHtml: Immediate treatment of symptomatic hyperviscosity in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia?
backHtml: Plasmapheresis, before systemic therapy; delay rituximab because of the IgM flare and defer red cell transfusion.

frontHtml: Which drug relieves splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms in primary myelofibrosis, and what is curative?
backHtml: Ruxolitinib for symptoms; allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is the only cure.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of localized gastric MALT lymphoma with H. pylori?
backHtml: Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy alone, with endoscopic follow-up; radiotherapy if disease persists.

frontHtml: High-risk tumor lysis prophylaxis, and one contraindication?
backHtml: Vigorous hydration plus rasburicase; rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because of hemolysis.

frontHtml: Which tests precede R-CHOP, and why?
backHtml: Cardiac function assessment before anthracycline, and hepatitis B serology before anti-CD20 therapy because of reactivation risk.

frontHtml: Treatment of early-stage mycosis fungoides?
backHtml: Treatment aimed at the skin itself: topical steroids, topical cytotoxic agents or retinoids, and ultraviolet light.

frontHtml: How do you correct the reticulocyte percentage for anemia?
backHtml: Multiply by patient hematocrit ÷ 45; the production index also divides by a maturation factor. An RPI below about 2 means underproduction.

frontHtml: What does hepcidin do to ferroportin, and what raises hepcidin?
backHtml: It binds ferroportin and causes its degradation, trapping iron in enterocytes and macrophages. IL-6 (inflammation) and iron loading raise it.

frontHtml: Iron deficiency versus anemia of inflammation: TIBC and ferritin?
backHtml: Iron deficiency: TIBC high, ferritin low. Inflammation: TIBC low or normal, ferritin normal or high.

frontHtml: Which three enzymes does lead inhibit, and what does each cause?
backHtml: ALA dehydratase (ALA rises), ferrochelatase (zinc protoporphyrin rises) and pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase (basophilic stippling).

frontHtml: What enzyme is mutated in X-linked sideroblastic anemia, and which vitamin is its cofactor?
backHtml: Erythroid ALA synthase (ALAS2); pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).

frontHtml: Name three acquired causes of ringed sideroblasts.
backHtml: Alcohol, isoniazid, copper deficiency (for example from excess zinc), lead, myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts.

frontHtml: What blood picture suggests myelophthisis?
backHtml: Leukoerythroblastic smear (nucleated red cells, immature myeloid cells) with teardrop cells.

frontHtml: Which B12-dependent enzyme explains a raised methylmalonic acid?
backHtml: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (adenosylcobalamin cofactor).

frontHtml: Which spinal cord tracts are damaged in subacute combined degeneration?
backHtml: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.

frontHtml: Why is serum gastrin high in pernicious anemia?
backHtml: Parietal cell loss causes achlorhydria, removing acid feedback on antral G cells.

frontHtml: How does nitrous oxide cause B12-deficiency myelopathy?
backHtml: It oxidises cobalamin's cobalt, inactivating methionine synthase; serum B12 may be normal.

frontHtml: Name three drugs that inhibit dihydrofolate reductase.
backHtml: Methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine.

frontHtml: What is the receptor for parvovirus B19 on erythroid progenitors?
backHtml: P antigen (globoside).

frontHtml: Which renal cells produce erythropoietin?
backHtml: Peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells of the cortex and outer medulla.

frontHtml: Which urine finding appears days after intravascular hemolysis and persists?
backHtml: Hemosiderinuria, from shed proximal tubular cells that reabsorbed free hemoglobin.

frontHtml: Warm versus cold AIHA: antibody class and DAT pattern?
backHtml: Warm: IgG, DAT IgG with or without C3. Cold: IgM, DAT C3 only.

frontHtml: Which infections cause transient cold agglutinins, and against which antigens?
backHtml: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (anti-I) and EBV (anti-i).

frontHtml: What gene is mutated in PNH, and which two proteins are lost?
backHtml: PIGA (GPI-anchor synthesis); CD55 and CD59.

frontHtml: Why can rasburicase cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency?
backHtml: Urate oxidation to allantoin generates hydrogen peroxide.

frontHtml: Why do patients with pyruvate kinase deficiency tolerate anemia well?
backHtml: Raised 2,3-BPG shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.

frontHtml: Name three drug mechanisms of immune hemolysis with an example of each.
backHtml: Hapten (high-dose penicillin), drug-dependent antibody (ceftriaxone, piperacillin), true autoantibody (methyldopa).

frontHtml: What substitution causes HbS, and when does it polymerise?
backHtml: β6 glutamate to valine; when deoxygenated.

frontHtml: Name four factors that promote HbS polymerisation.
backHtml: Low oxygen, acidosis, dehydration, raised 2,3-BPG, high HbS concentration, low HbF.

frontHtml: Why does sickle trait cause hematuria and nocturia?
backHtml: The hypoxic, hypertonic, acidic renal medulla sickles trait cells, causing papillary necrosis and hyposthenuria.

frontHtml: Which malignancy is linked to sickle trait?
backHtml: Renal medullary carcinoma.

frontHtml: What substitution causes HbC, and what does the smear show?
backHtml: β6 glutamate to lysine; target cells and rod-shaped crystals.

frontHtml: Newborn screen 'FS': what does it mean?
backHtml: HbF and HbS with no HbA: sickle cell disease (HbSS or HbS-β0-thalassemia).

frontHtml: How does hydroxyurea work in sickle cell disease?
backHtml: Ribonucleotide reductase inhibition raises HbF and lowers neutrophil count and adhesion.

frontHtml: Which α-thalassemia trait genotype can lead to Hb Bart's hydrops in offspring?
backHtml: Cis deletion (−−/αα), common in Southeast Asian ancestry.

frontHtml: What forms in HbH disease, and how many α genes are missing?
backHtml: β4 tetramers (HbH); three genes missing (−−/−α).

frontHtml: Which electrophoresis finding confirms β-thalassemia trait?
backHtml: HbA2 above about 3.5%.

frontHtml: Why does β-thalassemia intermedia cause iron overload without transfusions?
backHtml: Erythroferrone from expanded marrow suppresses hepcidin, increasing absorption.

frontHtml: Most common protein defect in hereditary spherocytosis?
backHtml: Ankyrin (vertical membrane-skeleton link).

frontHtml: Which enzyme is deficient in acute intermittent porphyria?
backHtml: Porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase).

frontHtml: Which enzyme is reduced in porphyria cutanea tarda, and what drives it?
backHtml: Hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, inhibited in the presence of hepatic iron.

frontHtml: Which ferritin level confirms iron deficiency in most adults?
backHtml: Below about 30 ng/mL.

frontHtml: Iron deficiency in a man or postmenopausal woman: next step?
backHtml: Bidirectional endoscopy (colonoscopy and upper endoscopy), plus celiac serology.

frontHtml: Why is once-daily or alternate-day oral iron preferred?
backHtml: Each dose raises hepcidin for about a day; spacing improves absorption and reduces GI effects.

frontHtml: Name four indications for intravenous iron.
backHtml: Malabsorption, active IBD, CKD (especially dialysis), oral intolerance or failure, ongoing large losses, late pregnancy.

frontHtml: In CKD, when is an iron trial reasonable?
backHtml: Transferrin saturation 30% or lower and ferritin 500 ng/mL or lower.

frontHtml: Why avoid ESA targets of 13 g/dL or more in CKD?
backHtml: More stroke, venous and access thrombosis and hypertension in trials.

frontHtml: Capillary blood lead above 3.5 µg/dL: next step?
backHtml: Confirm with a venous blood lead level.

frontHtml: Serum B12 is borderline: which test confirms deficiency?
backHtml: Methylmalonic acid (raised in B12 deficiency, normal in folate deficiency).

frontHtml: Treatment of pernicious anemia with neurologic signs?
backHtml: Intramuscular cyanocobalamin, frequent at first, then monthly for life.

frontHtml: What electrolyte can fall early in treatment of severe megaloblastic anemia?
backHtml: Potassium.

frontHtml: Folic acid dose to prevent recurrence after a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect?
backHtml: 4 mg daily from before conception.

frontHtml: Criteria for severe aplastic anemia?
backHtml: Cellularity below 25% plus two of: ANC below 500, platelets below 20,000, absolute reticulocytes below 60,000/mm3.

frontHtml: Young patient with severe aplastic anemia and a matched sibling: treatment?
backHtml: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

frontHtml: Chronic parvovirus B19 red cell aplasia in a transplant recipient: treatment?
backHtml: IVIG and reduction of immunosuppression.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of warm AIHA?
backHtml: Prednisone about 1 mg/kg/day with a slow taper.

frontHtml: Preferred second-line therapy for warm AIHA?
backHtml: Rituximab.

frontHtml: Why do steroids and splenectomy work poorly in cold agglutinin disease?
backHtml: Destruction is complement-mediated and mainly hepatic.

frontHtml: Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis with cytopenias: diagnostic test?
backHtml: Peripheral blood flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59, FLAER).

frontHtml: What must be given at least 2 weeks before eculizumab or ravulizumab?
backHtml: Meningococcal vaccines (MenACWY and MenB).

frontHtml: When should G6PD activity be measured after a hemolytic episode?
backHtml: About 3 months later; reticulocytes falsely raise it during recovery.

frontHtml: Name two drugs that need G6PD testing before use.
backHtml: Primaquine and tafenoquine (also rasburicase, dapsone where possible).

frontHtml: Penicillin prophylaxis in HbSS: when does it start and stop?
backHtml: From about 2 months to at least 5 years of age.

frontHtml: Who gets transcranial Doppler screening, and how often?
backHtml: Children with HbSS or HbS-β0-thalassemia, yearly from age 2 to 16.

frontHtml: Confirmed TCD velocity of 200 cm/s or more: management?
backHtml: Chronic transfusion program keeping HbS below about 30%.

frontHtml: From what age is hydroxyurea offered in HbSS?
backHtml: 9 months, regardless of symptoms.

frontHtml: Fever of 38.5 °C in a child with sickle cell disease: management?
backHtml: Cultures and prompt parenteral ceftriaxone without waiting for results.

frontHtml: Acute chest syndrome: empiric antibiotics?
backHtml: Parenteral cephalosporin plus a macrolide.

frontHtml: Upper hemoglobin limit after simple transfusion in sickle cell disease?
backHtml: About 10 g/dL, to avoid hyperviscosity.

frontHtml: Why check ferritin before interpreting HbA2?
backHtml: Iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask β-thalassemia trait.

frontHtml: Microcytosis with normal iron and normal HbA2: next test?
backHtml: α-Globin gene deletion analysis.

frontHtml: Which chelator needs weekly neutrophil counts?
backHtml: Deferiprone (agranulocytosis).

frontHtml: Which chelator needs audiology and eye checks?
backHtml: Deferoxamine.

frontHtml: Vaccines before splenectomy in hereditary spherocytosis, and timing?
backHtml: Pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, and Hib, at least 2 weeks before surgery.

frontHtml: Best initial test for a suspected acute porphyric attack?
backHtml: Spot urine porphobilinogen normalised to creatinine.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of porphyria cutanea tarda?
backHtml: Phlebotomy or low-dose hydroxychloroquine, plus removing triggers (alcohol, estrogen, HCV).

frontHtml: Why is the hemoglobin concentration near normal in the first hour after a large bleed?
backHtml: Whole blood is lost, so red cells and plasma leave in the same proportion; concentration is a ratio.

frontHtml: How long after an acute bleed does the hemoglobin reach its true new level?
backHtml: About 24 to 72 hours, once transcapillary refill and renal salt and water retention have restored plasma volume.

frontHtml: When do reticulocytes rise and peak after acute blood loss?
backHtml: They begin to rise after about 3 days and peak at about 1 week.

frontHtml: Which two white-cell and platelet changes commonly accompany acute hemorrhage?
backHtml: Neutrophilic leukocytosis and reactive thrombocytosis.

frontHtml: What membrane change produces target cells in cholestatic liver disease?
backHtml: Cholesterol and lecithin loading increases membrane surface area relative to cell volume.

frontHtml: What distinguishes spur cell anemia from target cells in liver disease?
backHtml: Spur cells (acanthocytes) come from excess free cholesterol that stiffens the membrane, causing splenic hemolysis and marking end-stage cirrhosis; target cells are harmless.

frontHtml: Why is the anemia of hypothyroidism hypoproliferative?
backHtml: Lower tissue oxygen demand reduces the erythropoietin drive, so production falls with the demand.

frontHtml: Which anemia features would a patient on alcohol show that reverse with abstinence?
backHtml: Round macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and ring sideroblasts after heavy drinking.

frontHtml: Why does hemoglobin fall in normal pregnancy?
backHtml: Plasma volume rises by about 40 to 50% while red cell mass rises by only about 20 to 30%.

frontHtml: What are the hemoglobin thresholds that define anemia in pregnancy by trimester?
backHtml: First trimester: under 11 g/dL. Second: under 10.5 g/dL. Third: under 11 g/dL again.

frontHtml: What causes the physiologic nadir of infancy, and when does it occur?
backHtml: Erythropoietin falls after birth as oxygenation rises; hemoglobin reaches about 9 to 11 g/dL at 2 to 3 months in term infants.

frontHtml: Name four reasons anemia of prematurity is deeper than the term nadir.
backHtml: Smaller iron stores, a blunted erythropoietin response, rapid growth, and repeated phlebotomy for laboratory tests.

frontHtml: Give three mechanisms by which excess cow's milk causes iron deficiency in toddlers.
backHtml: Low and poorly absorbed milk iron; calcium and casein inhibit non-heme iron absorption; milk volume displaces iron-rich foods (and, before 12 months, occult intestinal blood loss).

frontHtml: What distinguishes athletes' pseudoanemia from true iron deficiency in an athlete?
backHtml: Pseudoanemia has a normal MCV, normal ferritin and no symptoms; iron deficiency has low ferritin and often microcytosis.

frontHtml: What laboratory clue suggests mixed microcytic and macrocytic deficiency with a normal MCV?
backHtml: A high RDW with a dimorphic smear, often with hypersegmented neutrophils.

frontHtml: What are the three broad groups of causes of anemia in older adults?
backHtml: Nutritional deficiency, chronic kidney disease or inflammation, and unexplained anemia (some of which is early myelodysplastic syndrome).

frontHtml: How is the absolute neutrophil count calculated, and what value defines severe neutropenia?
backHtml: Total leukocytes multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands; severe is below 500/mm3.

frontHtml: Which three neutrophil pools exist, and which does the ANC measure?
backHtml: Marrow storage, marginated and circulating pools; the ANC measures only the circulating pool.

frontHtml: What is the Duffy-null associated neutrophil count, and why does it matter?
backHtml: Absent red cell Duffy antigen (ACKR1) with a lower circulating ANC but normal marrow reserve and no excess infection; recognising it avoids needless biopsy and drug withdrawal.

frontHtml: Which gene is mutated in cyclic neutropenia, and what is the cycle length?
backHtml: ELANE (neutrophil elastase), with nadirs about every 21 days.

frontHtml: Name the two mechanisms of drug-induced agranulocytosis.
backHtml: Immune destruction (hapten or immune complex) and direct toxicity to myeloid precursors.

frontHtml: Which drug classes classically cause agranulocytosis?
backHtml: Clozapine, thionamides (methimazole, propylthiouracil), sulfonamides including sulfasalazine, dapsone, procainamide and deferiprone.

frontHtml: Which organisms drive empiric therapy in febrile neutropenia?
backHtml: Gram-negative rods including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, so an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam is given promptly.

frontHtml: Which mechanism explains lymphopenia within hours of starting glucocorticoids?
backHtml: Redistribution of lymphocytes into lymphoid tissue and marrow (eosinophils fall at the same time).

frontHtml: Which non-immune mechanism of lymphopenia should be suspected with edema and low albumin?
backHtml: Loss of lymphocyte-rich lymph in intestinal lymphangiectasia or a thoracic duct leak.

frontHtml: What are the four mechanisms of thrombocytopenia, plus the artefact to exclude first?
backHtml: Reduced production, increased destruction or consumption, sequestration and dilution; exclude EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia.

frontHtml: How does EDTA cause pseudothrombocytopenia?
backHtml: It alters glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, exposing epitopes bound by naturally occurring antibodies that clump platelets in the tube; a citrate-tube count is normal.

frontHtml: Which antigens do ITP autoantibodies usually target, and how are platelets removed?
backHtml: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX; splenic macrophages clear the coated platelets through Fc-gamma receptors.

frontHtml: Why is platelet production low rather than high in ITP?
backHtml: The same antibodies and cytotoxic T cells damage megakaryocytes, and thrombopoietin is only normal or mildly raised.

frontHtml: Contrast the course of childhood and adult ITP.
backHtml: Childhood ITP is usually abrupt, post-viral and self-limited within months; adult ITP is usually insidious and chronic.

frontHtml: How do romiplostim and eltrombopag differ in how they bind the thrombopoietin receptor?
backHtml: Romiplostim is an injected peptide-antibody fusion binding the extracellular domain; eltrombopag is an oral small molecule binding the transmembrane domain.

frontHtml: Why must eltrombopag be separated from dairy, antacids and iron?
backHtml: It chelates polyvalent cations, which reduces its absorption.

frontHtml: Which platelet antigen is most often involved in neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia?
backHtml: HPA-1a, with maternal IgG against the paternally inherited antigen; the mother's own count is normal.

frontHtml: Which single test best separates polycythemia vera from secondary erythrocytosis?
backHtml: Serum erythropoietin: suppressed in PV, normal or high in secondary causes.

frontHtml: Which mutations drive polycythemia vera?
backHtml: JAK2 V617F in about 95%, with JAK2 exon 12 mutations in most of the rest.

frontHtml: What is aquagenic pruritus, and in which disease is it characteristic?
backHtml: Intense itching after a warm bath or shower, attributed to clonal basophils and mast cells; characteristic of polycythemia vera.

frontHtml: Which unusual thrombosis sites should prompt JAK2 testing?
backHtml: Splanchnic veins: hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal and mesenteric veins.

frontHtml: What hematocrit target is used in polycythemia vera, and why?
backHtml: Below 45%, because it lowers cardiovascular death and major thrombosis compared with a looser target.

frontHtml: Which patients with PV receive cytoreduction, and with what first-line drug?
backHtml: High-risk patients (age 60 or older, or prior thrombosis); hydroxyurea, with interferon preferred in younger patients and pregnancy.

frontHtml: Give four causes of inappropriate (autonomous) erythropoietin secretion.
backHtml: Renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma and uterine leiomyoma (also pheochromocytoma and renal cysts).

frontHtml: Why can pulse oximetry be normal in a smoker with hypoxic erythrocytosis?
backHtml: Standard two-wavelength oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin; co-oximetry measures it.

frontHtml: Which drugs raise the hematocrit?
backHtml: Testosterone and anabolic steroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and SGLT2 inhibitors.

frontHtml: Which cytokine links inflammation to reactive thrombocytosis?
backHtml: Interleukin-6, which raises hepatic thrombopoietin production.

frontHtml: Name the three driver mutations of essential thrombocythemia.
backHtml: JAK2 V617F, CALR and MPL; all activate JAK2-STAT signalling through the thrombopoietin receptor.

frontHtml: Which test must be negative before essential thrombocythemia is diagnosed?
backHtml: BCR-ABL1, because CML can present with isolated thrombocytosis.

frontHtml: Why does bleeding occur at platelet counts above about 1,000,000/mm3?
backHtml: Large von Willebrand multimers adsorb to the platelet surface and are cleared, causing acquired von Willebrand syndrome.

frontHtml: How do glucocorticoids raise the neutrophil count?
backHtml: Mainly by demargination (reduced adhesion molecule expression), plus faster marrow release and slower migration into tissue.

frontHtml: Which smear features favour a leukemoid reaction over CML?
backHtml: Toxic granulation, Döhle bodies and vacuoles, mature neutrophils without basophilia, and a high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score.

frontHtml: Which cytokine drives eosinophil production?
backHtml: Interleukin-5, from type 2 helper T cells and innate lymphoid cells.

frontHtml: Which organ damage is most feared in hypereosinophilic syndrome?
backHtml: Cardiac: endomyocardial necrosis with mural thrombus, then fibrosis causing restrictive cardiomyopathy.

frontHtml: Which fusion gene makes hypereosinophilia imatinib-responsive?
backHtml: FIP1L1-PDGFRA, from a small interstitial deletion on chromosome 4.

frontHtml: What venous hematocrit defines neonatal polycythemia, and which metabolic problem accompanies it?
backHtml: Above 65%; hypoglycemia (with jaundice from the larger red cell mass).

frontHtml: What drives the decision to transfuse in acute hemorrhage?
backHtml: Hemodynamics and ongoing loss, not the first hemoglobin, which lags until plasma volume is restored.

frontHtml: What is the usual restrictive transfusion trigger for stable hospitalized adults?
backHtml: A hemoglobin below 7 g/dL, including critically ill patients and those with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

frontHtml: Which patients use a transfusion trigger of about 8 g/dL?
backHtml: Those with pre-existing cardiovascular disease, and patients undergoing orthopedic or cardiac surgery (some guidance uses 7.5 g/dL in cardiac surgery).

frontHtml: By how much does one unit of packed red cells raise the hemoglobin in a stable adult?
backHtml: About 1 g/dL (hematocrit about 3%); give one unit and reassess.

frontHtml: What product ratio is used in a massive transfusion protocol for hemorrhagic shock?
backHtml: Approximately 1:1:1 plasma, platelets and red cells, with tranexamic acid in trauma within 3 hours of injury.

frontHtml: Why is large-volume crystalloid avoided in hemorrhagic shock?
backHtml: It dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis and hypothermia.

frontHtml: What is the definitive treatment of spur cell anemia?
backHtml: Liver transplantation; transfusion gives only short-lived benefit.

frontHtml: Which five causes should be sought for anemia in cirrhosis?
backHtml: Gastrointestinal blood loss, iron deficiency, folate deficiency, hypersplenism and hemolysis (plus drug effects).

frontHtml: Which cause of anemia in pregnancy is most likely, and which test confirms it?
backHtml: Iron deficiency; ferritin, with a value below about 30 ng/mL confirming deficiency in pregnancy.

frontHtml: When is intravenous iron used in pregnancy?
backHtml: In the second or third trimester when oral iron fails or is not tolerated, or when the deficit is large close to delivery.

frontHtml: When do exclusively breastfed term and preterm infants start iron supplementation?
backHtml: Term infants from about 4 months until iron-rich complementary foods are established; preterm infants from about the first month.

frontHtml: At what age is universal hemoglobin screening performed in children?
backHtml: At about 12 months, with assessment of risk factors.

frontHtml: What milk limit and iron dose are used for toddler iron deficiency?
backHtml: Limit cow's milk to about 16 to 24 oz (500 to 700 mL) daily and give about 3 mg/kg/day of elemental iron between meals.

frontHtml: What confirms the diagnosis after starting iron in a toddler, and for how long is iron continued?
backHtml: A hemoglobin rise of at least 1 g/dL in about 4 weeks; continue for about 3 months after the count normalises.

frontHtml: What does iron deficiency in an older adult or postmenopausal woman require?
backHtml: Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy to look for occult malignancy or another source, even if stool testing is negative.

frontHtml: Which common medications contribute to anemia in older adults?
backHtml: Proton pump inhibitors and metformin (B12 absorption), antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulants (blood loss), methotrexate and some antiepileptics (folate).

frontHtml: Which four questions frame an incidentally low neutrophil count?
backHtml: Is the patient infected? Are other lineages low? Is a drug responsible? Is the pattern long-standing and stable?

frontHtml: How is cyclic neutropenia confirmed?
backHtml: Serial blood counts two to three times a week for about 6 weeks, showing nadirs roughly every 21 days.

frontHtml: What are the first steps in suspected drug-induced agranulocytosis?
backHtml: Stop the drug at once and, if febrile, draw cultures and give empiric intravenous anti-pseudomonal antibiotics; G-CSF for severe cases.

frontHtml: Why is switching from methimazole to propylthiouracil unsafe after agranulocytosis?
backHtml: The thionamides cross-react; definitive therapy with radioactive iodine or surgery is chosen instead.

frontHtml: Define febrile neutropenia.
backHtml: A single oral temperature of 38.3 °C (101 °F) or more, or 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) for an hour, with an ANC below 500 or expected to fall below 500.

frontHtml: When is vancomycin added in febrile neutropenia?
backHtml: For hemodynamic instability, suspected catheter or skin infection, pneumonia, or known MRSA colonisation.

frontHtml: Which smear finding suggests marrow infiltration in pancytopenia?
backHtml: A leukoerythroblastic picture: nucleated red cells, immature myeloid cells and teardrop cells.

frontHtml: Which nutritional causes of pancytopenia must be excluded before marrow biopsy?
backHtml: Vitamin B12, folate and copper deficiency.

frontHtml: What precautions apply to an infant with an abnormal newborn TREC screen?
backHtml: Avoid live vaccines including rotavirus, and give only irradiated, leukoreduced, CMV-safe blood products until immune status is known.

frontHtml: Which infections should be tested for in a new adult diagnosis of ITP?
backHtml: HIV and hepatitis C, because both cause secondary ITP and treating them can raise the count.

frontHtml: When is a bone marrow biopsy indicated in suspected ITP?
backHtml: For atypical features: other cytopenias, an abnormal smear, splenomegaly or failure to respond. Age alone is not an indication.

frontHtml: Which children with new ITP are observed rather than treated?
backHtml: Those with skin bleeding only (petechiae and bruising), whatever the platelet count.

frontHtml: What is first-line treatment for newly diagnosed adult ITP with platelets below 30,000/mm3 or bleeding?
backHtml: Glucocorticoids: prednisone for no more than about 6 weeks including taper, or short-course high-dose dexamethasone.

frontHtml: What is given for life-threatening bleeding in ITP?
backHtml: Platelet transfusion plus IVIG plus high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids together.

frontHtml: Name the second-line options for steroid-dependent ITP.
backHtml: A thrombopoietin-receptor agonist (eltrombopag, romiplostim, avatrombopag), rituximab, splenectomy (usually delayed at least 12 months), and fostamatinib later.

frontHtml: How does gestational thrombocytopenia differ from ITP in pregnancy?
backHtml: It appears late, is usually above 70,000/mm3, has no prior history or bleeding, carries no fetal risk, and resolves after delivery.

frontHtml: How is severe neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia treated?
backHtml: Platelet transfusion without delay (antigen-negative units if available), often with IVIG, plus cranial ultrasonography.

frontHtml: Which drugs can raise the platelet count before procedures in chronic liver disease?
backHtml: Oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonists approved for that setting: avatrombopag and lusutrombopag.

frontHtml: Which two tests are sent together first for unexplained erythrocytosis?
backHtml: Serum erythropoietin and JAK2 V617F.

frontHtml: What is tested if JAK2 V617F is negative but erythropoietin is low?
backHtml: A JAK2 exon 12 mutation.

frontHtml: What two treatments does every patient with polycythemia vera receive?
backHtml: Phlebotomy to a hematocrit below 45% and low-dose aspirin, unless contraindicated.

frontHtml: Should iron be given for the microcytosis of phlebotomy-treated PV?
backHtml: No: the iron deficiency limits red cell production, and replacement raises the hematocrit again.

frontHtml: Which cytoreductive drug is preferred in younger patients or pregnancy with PV?
backHtml: Interferon alfa (ropeginterferon alfa-2b), because it is not teratogenic.

frontHtml: How is erythrocytosis from hypoxic lung disease or sleep apnea managed?
backHtml: Treat the cause (CPAP, oxygen when criteria are met, smoking cessation); phlebotomy only for symptomatic hyperviscosity.

frontHtml: Why is routine phlebotomy avoided in cyanotic congenital heart disease?
backHtml: It causes iron deficiency and worsens oxygen delivery; it is used only for hyperviscosity symptoms, with fluid replacement.

frontHtml: How is testosterone-associated erythrocytosis monitored and managed?
backHtml: Hematocrit at baseline, at 3 to 6 months and then yearly; above about 54%, stop the drug, look for hypoxia or sleep apnea, and restart at a lower dose once it falls.

frontHtml: Which drug class lowers the hematocrit in post-transplant erythrocytosis?
backHtml: ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers.

frontHtml: Which tests are sent for unexplained persistent thrombocytosis?
backHtml: Ferritin and iron studies and CRP for reactive causes; then JAK2 V617F, CALR, MPL and BCR-ABL1, with marrow examination.

frontHtml: How is low-risk essential thrombocythemia managed?
backHtml: Observation or low-dose aspirin, with aspirin favoured when there is a JAK2 mutation or cardiovascular risk factors.

frontHtml: How is high-risk essential thrombocythemia managed?
backHtml: Aspirin plus hydroxyurea, with interferon or anagrelide as alternatives.

frontHtml: What is checked before starting aspirin when platelets exceed about 1,000,000/mm3?
backHtml: Von Willebrand factor activity (ristocetin cofactor); if it is low, aspirin raises bleeding risk.

frontHtml: Which features of a high leukocyte count point to a myeloid neoplasm rather than a leukemoid reaction?
backHtml: Splenomegaly, basophilia, eosinophilia, a myelocyte peak, blasts, or no reactive trigger; test peripheral blood for BCR-ABL1.

frontHtml: Which infection must be excluded or treated before giving glucocorticoids to a patient with eosinophilia?
backHtml: Strongyloidiasis; give ivermectin, because steroids can cause hyperinfection with gram-negative sepsis.

frontHtml: Which organ assessment is essential in hypereosinophilia?
backHtml: Cardiac: troponin, ECG and echocardiography for endomyocardial disease and mural thrombus.

frontHtml: Which drug is used for steroid sparing in idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome?
backHtml: Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5); hydroxyurea and interferon are other options.

frontHtml: Why must a high neonatal capillary hematocrit be rechecked venously?
backHtml: Capillary samples read several points higher; polycythemia is defined by a venous hematocrit above 65%.

frontHtml: When is partial exchange transfusion used in neonatal polycythemia?
backHtml: Only for symptomatic hyperviscosity (lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, seizures), replacing blood with normal saline.

frontHtml: Which factors does the PT measure?
backHtml: Factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen (extrinsic and common pathways).

frontHtml: Why do warfarin and early vitamin K deficiency prolong the PT before the aPTT?
backHtml: Factor VII has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors (a few hours).

frontHtml: A prolonged aPTT corrects on 1:1 mixing. What does that mean?
backHtml: A factor deficiency (VIII, IX, XI or XII), not an inhibitor.

frontHtml: Mixing study corrects at first but prolongs again after 1–2 h at 37 °C: what is present?
backHtml: A time-dependent factor VIII inhibitor (autoantibody), as in acquired hemophilia A.

frontHtml: Which factor deficiencies prolong the aPTT but cause no bleeding?
backHtml: Factor XII, prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen.

frontHtml: Name four bleeding disorders with normal PT and aPTT.
backHtml: Platelet function defects, most von Willebrand disease, factor XIII deficiency and vascular fragility (e.g. scurvy); also α2-antiplasmin or PAI-1 deficiency.

frontHtml: Hemophilia severity by factor activity?
backHtml: Severe below 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild above 5% to below 40%.

frontHtml: Typical bleeding sites in severe hemophilia?
backHtml: Joints (hemarthroses) and deep muscles; intracranial hemorrhage is the main cause of death.

frontHtml: Which von Willebrand disease type can develop thrombocytopenia with desmopressin?
backHtml: Type 2B (gain-of-function binding to platelet GpIb).

frontHtml: Which von Willebrand disease type mimics hemophilia A but is autosomal?
backHtml: Type 2N: vWF cannot bind factor VIII, so factor VIII is low.

frontHtml: Umbilical stump bleeding with normal PT, aPTT, platelets and fibrinogen: likely factor deficiency and confirmatory finding?
backHtml: Factor XIII deficiency; clot dissolves in 5 mol/L urea and factor XIII activity is low.

frontHtml: Which reaction does vitamin K support, and which proteins depend on it?
backHtml: γ-Carboxylation of glutamate residues on factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S.

frontHtml: What timing defines late vitamin K deficiency bleeding?
backHtml: 2–12 weeks of age, mainly in exclusively breastfed infants without prophylaxis or with cholestasis; often intracranial.

frontHtml: Bernard-Soulier syndrome: missing receptor and smear finding?
backHtml: GpIb-IX-V (vWF receptor); mild thrombocytopenia with giant platelets.

frontHtml: Glanzmann thrombasthenia: aggregation pattern?
backHtml: No aggregation with ADP, collagen, epinephrine or arachidonic acid; normal ristocetin response; absent clot retraction.

frontHtml: How does adding normal plasma separate vWD from Bernard-Soulier syndrome on ristocetin testing?
backHtml: Normal plasma corrects the ristocetin response in vWD (supplies vWF) but not in Bernard-Soulier (receptor missing).

frontHtml: Which coagulation factor is low in DIC but normal or high in liver disease?
backHtml: Factor VIII.

frontHtml: Main initiating mechanism of sepsis-associated DIC?
backHtml: Cytokine- and endotoxin-induced tissue factor expression on monocytes and endothelium.

frontHtml: Why can fibrinogen look normal early in septic DIC?
backHtml: Fibrinogen is an acute phase reactant; serial falling values matter more than one level.

frontHtml: Factor V Leiden versus prothrombin G20210A: mechanisms?
backHtml: Factor V Leiden: factor Va resists cleavage by activated protein C. G20210A: 3′ UTR variant raises prothrombin levels.

frontHtml: Which inherited thrombophilia causes heparin resistance?
backHtml: Antithrombin deficiency (heparin acts by potentiating antithrombin).

frontHtml: What does activated protein C (with protein S) inactivate?
backHtml: Factors Va and VIIIa.

frontHtml: Three acquired causes of low antithrombin?
backHtml: Nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss), liver disease, L-asparaginase (also DIC and heparin consumption).

frontHtml: How do antiphospholipid antibodies affect the aPTT and the patient?
backHtml: They prolong the aPTT in vitro (lupus anticoagulant, not corrected by mixing) but cause arterial and venous thrombosis and pregnancy loss in vivo.

frontHtml: Why does unfractionated heparin inhibit thrombin but LMWH mostly not?
backHtml: Inhibiting thrombin requires a chain long enough to bridge antithrombin and thrombin; LMWH chains are mostly too short, so they act mainly on Xa.

frontHtml: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis suggests which underlying condition?
backHtml: Occult visceral adenocarcinoma, classically pancreatic (Trousseau syndrome).

frontHtml: Antibody and effector mechanism in ABO-incompatible transfusion?
backHtml: Preformed IgM anti-A/anti-B activating complement → intravascular hemolysis.

frontHtml: Timing and mechanism of a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction?
backHtml: 3–14 days; anamnestic IgG alloantibody (often Kidd, Rh, Kell, Duffy) → extravascular hemolysis.

frontHtml: TRALI mechanism?
backHtml: Donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies activate primed recipient neutrophils in the lung → noncardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 h.

frontHtml: Which product modification prevents TA-GVHD?
backHtml: Irradiation (or pathogen reduction) of cellular products; leukoreduction is not enough.

frontHtml: Why are platelets the product most often bacterially contaminated?
backHtml: They are stored at room temperature (20–24 °C).

frontHtml: Which organism classically contaminates refrigerated red cells?
backHtml: Yersinia enterocolitica.

frontHtml: Mechanism of hypocalcemia in massive transfusion?
backHtml: Citrate anticoagulant chelates ionized calcium.

frontHtml: Suspected joint or head bleed in severe hemophilia: what comes first?
backHtml: Factor concentrate replacement, before imaging or other tests.

frontHtml: Which hemophilia patients can be treated with desmopressin?
backHtml: Mild hemophilia A with a documented response (not hemophilia B or severe A).

frontHtml: Treatment of acute bleeding with a high-titer factor VIII inhibitor?
backHtml: Bypassing agent: recombinant factor VIIa or activated prothrombin complex concentrate.

frontHtml: Acquired hemophilia A: two arms of treatment?
backHtml: Hemostasis (bypassing agents or recombinant porcine factor VIII) and eradicating the antibody (glucocorticoids ± cyclophosphamide or rituximab).

frontHtml: Why are women with type 1 vWD at risk of delayed postpartum hemorrhage?
backHtml: vWF and factor VIII rise in pregnancy but fall quickly after delivery.

frontHtml: When is tranexamic acid avoided in hemophilia?
backHtml: Upper urinary tract bleeding (hematuria): risk of obstructing clots.

frontHtml: Standard newborn vitamin K prophylaxis?
backHtml: A single intramuscular dose of vitamin K soon after birth.

frontHtml: Should INR or platelets be corrected before paracentesis in cirrhosis?
backHtml: No; prophylactic plasma or platelets are not recommended for low-risk procedures.

frontHtml: Bleeding DIC with fibrinogen below about 150 mg/dL despite plasma: give what?
backHtml: Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.

frontHtml: When is heparin used in DIC?
backHtml: When thrombosis predominates: purpura fulminans, large-vessel thrombosis, chronic DIC of cancer, retained dead fetus.

frontHtml: Fast-acting treatment for uremic bleeding before an urgent procedure?
backHtml: Desmopressin (onset about 1 hour); dialysis and anemia correction help longer term.

frontHtml: Which drug gives longer-lasting control of recurrent uremic bleeding?
backHtml: Conjugated estrogens (onset over days, effect about 2 weeks).

frontHtml: Scurvy treatment and key lab finding?
backHtml: Oral vitamin C; platelets and coagulation tests are normal.

frontHtml: Wells DVT score cutoff for "DVT likely"?
backHtml: 2 or more.

frontHtml: First test when DVT is unlikely?
backHtml: High-sensitivity D-dimer; negative excludes DVT.

frontHtml: First test when DVT is likely?
backHtml: Compression ultrasonography (D-dimer cannot exclude DVT).

frontHtml: Negative proximal-only ultrasound in a high-probability patient: next?
backHtml: D-dimer or repeat ultrasound in about a week.

frontHtml: Age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff for suspected PE over age 50?
backHtml: Age × 10 µg/L (FEU).

frontHtml: Imaging and treatment for suspected DVT in pregnancy?
backHtml: Compression ultrasonography (with iliac Doppler if needed); treat with LMWH.

frontHtml: Anticoagulant of choice for VTE in pregnancy?
backHtml: Low-molecular-weight heparin.

frontHtml: Anticoagulant required with a mechanical heart valve?
backHtml: Warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated.

frontHtml: Preferred long-term anticoagulant in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome?
backHtml: Warfarin (target INR 2–3).

frontHtml: Duration after VTE provoked by surgery?
backHtml: 3 months, then stop.

frontHtml: Duration after a first unprovoked proximal DVT or PE with low bleeding risk?
backHtml: Extended (no planned stop date), reassessed at least yearly.

frontHtml: Rule for starting warfarin for acute VTE?
backHtml: Overlap with heparin for at least 5 days and until INR is 2 or higher for 24 hours.

frontHtml: Why not test protein C, S and antithrombin at VTE diagnosis?
backHtml: Levels fall with acute thrombosis and anticoagulants, giving false positives.

frontHtml: Only indication for an IVC filter in acute VTE?
backHtml: Acute proximal DVT or PE with a contraindication to anticoagulation.

frontHtml: Restrictive red cell transfusion threshold for most stable inpatients?
backHtml: Hemoglobin below 7 g/dL; transfuse one unit and reassess.

frontHtml: Prophylactic platelet threshold in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia?
backHtml: Below 10,000/mm<sup>3</sup>.

frontHtml: Platelet thresholds for central line and lumbar puncture?
backHtml: Central line below 20,000/mm<sup>3</sup>; lumbar puncture below 50,000/mm<sup>3</sup>.

frontHtml: Main components of cryoprecipitate?
backHtml: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII and fibronectin.

frontHtml: Only transfusion reaction in which the unit may be restarted?
backHtml: Mild isolated urticaria, after an antihistamine once symptoms resolve.

frontHtml: TACO versus TRALI: blood pressure and response to diuretics?
backHtml: TACO: hypertension, high BNP, responds to diuretics. TRALI: often hypotension, normal filling pressures, no diuretic benefit.

frontHtml: Fever and hypotension during platelet transfusion: steps?
backHtml: Stop, culture patient and bag, start broad-spectrum antibiotics, notify blood bank.

frontHtml: Target product ratio in massive transfusion?
backHtml: Plasma:platelets:red cells about 1:1:1 (or whole blood).

frontHtml: Time window for tranexamic acid in trauma?
backHtml: Within 3 hours of injury.

frontHtml: The lethal triad and its fourth corner?
backHtml: Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy; plus hypocalcemia.

frontHtml: Permissive hypotension target and its main contraindication?
backHtml: Systolic about 80–90 mm Hg until bleeding is controlled; not in traumatic brain injury.

frontHtml: Four criteria in the simple trauma score for massive transfusion?
backHtml: Penetrating mechanism, systolic pressure 90 mm Hg or less, heart rate 120/min or more, positive FAST (2 or more predicts need).

frontHtml: Why does hyperkalemia occur with massive transfusion?
backHtml: Potassium leaks from stored (especially older or irradiated) red cells.

frontHtml: Why is the direct antiglobulin test negative in fragmentation hemolysis?
backHtml: Cells are destroyed by physical shear, heat or fibrin strands, not by antibody or complement on the membrane.

frontHtml: Name three schistocyte shapes seen on a smear.
backHtml: Helmet cells, triangular fragments and keratocytes (horn cells); microspherocytes often accompany them.

frontHtml: Fragments plus a normal platelet count: where do you look?
backHtml: For a macrovascular source: a leaking or stenotic valve, an assist device, or repetitive external impact (march hemoglobinuria).

frontHtml: Which urine findings mark intravascular hemolysis?
backHtml: Dipstick positive for blood with few or no red cells (hemoglobinuria), and hemosiderinuria a few days later.

frontHtml: Why can a leaking prosthetic valve cause iron deficiency?
backHtml: Chronic loss of filtered hemoglobin and shed hemosiderin-laden tubular cells drains iron in the urine.

frontHtml: What does the Shiga toxin A subunit do inside the cell?
backHtml: It removes an adenine from 28S rRNA of the 60S subunit, halting protein synthesis.

frontHtml: Caplacizumab binds what, and what does that prevent?
backHtml: The A1 domain of von Willebrand factor, preventing vWF binding to platelet GPIb and new microthrombi.

frontHtml: How does severe aortic stenosis or an LVAD cause mucosal bleeding?
backHtml: Shear unfolds vWF so ADAMTS13 cleaves its largest multimers: acquired von Willebrand syndrome.

frontHtml: From which embryonic structure does the spleen develop?
backHtml: Mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium (mesoderm), though it is supplied by the celiac trunk.

frontHtml: Which ligament carries the splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail?
backHtml: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament.

frontHtml: Where are T cells and B cells in the white pulp?
backHtml: T cells in the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath; B cells in follicles and the marginal zone.

frontHtml: Define splenic culling and pitting.
backHtml: Culling: macrophages engulf whole old or rigid red cells. Pitting: inclusions are removed and the cell returns to circulation.

frontHtml: What are Howell-Jolly bodies, and what do they indicate?
backHtml: Nuclear DNA remnants in red cells; their presence indicates absent or poor splenic function.

frontHtml: Why do asplenic patients get fulminant pneumococcal sepsis?
backHtml: Loss of marginal-zone macrophage clearance and T-cell-independent IgM responses to capsular polysaccharide.

frontHtml: Name two nonsurgical causes of hyposplenism.
backHtml: Sickle cell anemia (autosplenectomy) and celiac disease; others include SLE, amyloidosis and alcohol-related liver disease.

frontHtml: List four causes of massive splenomegaly.
